meta-title.text: canvas-watch — which background is your floating element over?

meta-description.text: Works out which background zone a floating element sits over and puts that answer on it as a class. Framework-agnostic core, optional Svelte adapter.

meta-og-description.text: Work out which background zone a floating element sits over, and get that answer as a class. What you restyle with it is up to you.

hero-eyebrow.text: Framework-agnostic core · optional Svelte adapter · ISC

hero-h1.text: Tell a floating element which background it's over.
hero-h1.approvedText: Tell a floating element which background it's over.

hero-lede.text: A sticky header crosses a dark hero, then a white section, then a photo. canvas-watch works out which zone it's sitting over and puts that answer on the element as a class.

hero-support.text: That's the whole library — one class, kept in step as things move. Re-tint a shadow, flip ink from dark to light, swap a border, invert the entire panel. The styling is yours.

hero-figure-caption.text: The card straddles two zones. The one covering most of it wins, and its name lands on the card as a class. The bar at the top of this page is doing it for real — scroll, and read the class it's wearing.

tryit-intro.text:
Try it

Scroll inside the frame. The floating panel holds three regions, each one separately watched, and the cells behind them change colour across the row as well as down the stack. Wherever the panel spans a boundary, its regions disagree — each takes the ink of whatever is under it.

tryit-second.text: It needs nothing from the library beyond registering each region — one watcher resolves them all in the same frame.

demo-note-primary.text: Nothing coordinates those three regions: they're three watched elements sharing one watcher, resolving in the same frame. Each resolved against the cell under itself.

demo-note-secondary.text: Drag the threshold to 1.00 and a region has to sit entirely within one cell before it takes anything, so any region straddling a boundary falls back to no class at all. The cells can't be page-level triggers, incidentally — they're inside a scroller, and a clipped cell still reports a full-size rect. Invisible proxy strips outside the scroller carry the trigger instead, one per column, relabelled as you scroll.

demo-code-intro.text:
The code running above

This demo builds its own watcher rather than joining the shared one, because threshold is set at construction and the slider changes it. Its selectors are deliberately distinct — -demozone, not -trigger — so the page's own watcher never resolves these bands and the header stays out of it.

why-io-heading-lede.text:
Why not just use an IntersectionObserver?

Because it can't answer this question — and because canvas-watch is already using one for the part it is good at.

why-io-cant.text:
What IntersectionObserver can't do

An IntersectionObserver measures a target against a root, and that root has to be an ancestor of the target, or the viewport. That is the whole model.

"Is this floating card mostly over that background band?" involves two elements with no ancestor relationship at all — they are siblings, or cousins, or in unrelated parts of the tree. There is no root you can pass that expresses it, and no threshold array that recovers it. The answer you want is the overlap of two arbitrary rectangles, which is a different question from the one IO was built to answer.

why-io-instead.text:
So what does it do instead?

It compares getBoundingClientRect() on the watched element and on each candidate zone, takes the area of the intersection as a fraction of the watched element's own area, and applies the threshold and nesting rules. Plain geometry, once per frame.

why-io-expensive-half.text:
IntersectionObserver still does the expensive half

Rectangle math is cheap; doing it for every element on a long page, every frame, is not. So canvas-watch keeps two IntersectionObservers whose only job is to decide what is worth measuring:

[table] Observer / Watches / Effect
Element gate — Every watched element — An element off screen is dropped from the measured set entirely. Its rect is never read and its class is cleared.
Zone gate — Every trigger zone, with a triggerRootMargin of 200px by default — Only zones near the viewport stay candidates, so a page with two hundred zones compares against the handful currently in play.

The result is that per-frame cost tracks what is on screen rather than how long the document is, and a page with nothing visible to resolve schedules no work at all. IO is doing what it is genuinely good at — cheap, off-main-thread visibility signals — and the rectangle comparison only runs on what survives that filter.
